title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt XXX: The Tale Retold (lines 2093–2143)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 78–80, lines 2093–2143 (fitt XXX). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Klaeber prints the section numeral [XXVIIII–XXX] at line 2039 and marks no new section at line 2093; the division between fitts XXIX and XXX at 2093 is ours. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Tō lang ys tō reccenne, hū i(c ð)ām lēodsceaðan
yfla gehwylces ondlēan forgeald;
sentences.l: Too long it is to be told, how I to the people-scather of each of evils requital repaid;
sentences.i: It would take too long to tell how I paid that scourge of the people back for every one of his evils;
sentences.n: Klaeber prints the section numeral [XXVIIII–XXX] at line 2039 and marks no break at 2093; the division at 2093 is ours. ‘Tō lang ys tō reccenne’ is ‘too long is to be told’: ‘reccenne’ is the inflected infinitive (‘tō’ + ‘-enne’) of ‘reccan’, ‘tell’, with a passive sense, and Sievers, Holthausen, Schücking and Sedgefield would print the plain ‘reccan’ (apparatus). The ‘hū’ clause names what is too long to tell, ‘how I … repaid’: ‘forgeald’ is the past of ‘forgieldan’, ‘pay back’, the payment is ‘ondlēan’, ‘requital’, and ‘yfla gehwylces’ is a genitive, ‘for each of evils’. The parentheses in ‘i(c ð)ām’ mark letters Klaeber supplies; the manuscript reads ‘huiedā’, and Grundtvig’s transcript and Kemble give ‘hū ic ðām’. The italic ‘o’ of ‘ondlēan’ marks a change: the manuscript has ‘hond’, ‘hand’, and Grein (with a query), Rieger, Holthausen, Schücking and Chambers read ‘ond-’, the prefix ‘in return’ (the apparatus refers to 1541). ‘lēodsceaðan’ is the dative ‘people-scather’, Grendel; ‘sceaða’ is the ‘scather’ of ‘mānscaða’, ‘crime-scather’. Beowulf is speaking to Higelāc, and the fight with Grendel in the hall has just been told.

sentences.t:
þǣr ic, þēoden mīn, þīne lēode
weorðode weorcum.
sentences.l: there I, my lord, your people honoured with deeds.
sentences.i: There, my lord, I did honour to your people by my deeds.
sentences.n: ‘þǣr’ is ‘there’, in Heorot, in the fighting. ‘þēoden mīn’ is a vocative, ‘my lord’, Beowulf addressing Higelāc. ‘þīne lēode’, ‘your people’, is the accusative object of ‘weorðode’, ‘honoured’, from ‘weorðian’, and ‘weorcum’ is a dative of means, ‘with deeds’.

sentences.t:
Hē on weg losade,
lȳtle hwīle līfwynna br(ēa)c;
sentences.l: He away slipped, a little while of life-joys enjoyed;
sentences.i: He slipped away, and enjoyed the pleasures of life for only a little while;
sentences.n: ‘Hē’ is Grendel. ‘on weg losade’ is ‘slipped away’: ‘losian’ is ‘be lost, escape’ and ‘on weg’ is ‘away’. ‘lȳtle hwīle’ is an accusative of time, ‘for a little while’, and ‘līfwynna’ is the genitive plural ‘of life-joys’ that ‘brūcan’, ‘enjoy’, governs. In ‘br(ēa)c’ the parentheses mark letters Klaeber restores because the manuscript is damaged there: one Thorkelin transcript reads ‘bræc’ and the other ‘brene’ altered to ‘brec’, and Kemble’s ‘brēac’ is the past of ‘brūcan’.

sentences.t:
hwæþre him sīo swīðre swaðe weardade
hand on Hiorte, ond hē hēan ðonan,
mōdes geōmor meregrund gefēoll.
sentences.l: yet to him the stronger in the track stayed, the hand, in Heorot, and he, humbled, thence, sad of mind, to the mere-bottom fell.
sentences.i: But his right hand stayed behind on his trail, the hand in Heorot, and he, brought low and heavy at heart, from there fell to the bottom of the mere.
sentences.n: ‘hwæþre’ is ‘yet, however’: Grendel escaped, but without his arm. The subject of ‘weardade’ is ‘hand’, and ‘sīo swīðre’, ‘the stronger (hand)’, the right, stands far before it, agreeing with it across the verb (my ‘l’ keeps that order and supplies no word): ‘swīðre’ is the comparative of ‘swīð’, ‘strong’. ‘him’ is a dative, ‘to him’, and ‘swaðe’ a dative, ‘in the track’; ‘weardade’ is the past of ‘weardian’, ‘guard, hold, remain’, and ‘stayed behind on his trail’ is my guess, since the construction is odd. ‘hēan’ is ‘humbled, abject’, ‘ðonan’ ‘from there’, and ‘mōdes geōmor’ ‘sad of mind’, the genitive saying in what respect. ‘meregrund’ is ‘mere-bottom’, an accusative of goal that needs no preposition after ‘gefēoll’, ‘fell’ (compare ‘meregrundas’, ‘mere-bottoms’, at 1449).

sentences.t:
Mē þone wælrǣs wine Scildunga
fǣttan golde fela lēanode,
manegum māðmum, syððan mergen cōm,
ond wē tō symble geseten hæfdon.
sentences.l: To me for that slaughter-rush the friend of the Scyldings with adorned gold much rewarded, with many treasures, after morning came and we to the feast sat down had.
sentences.i: For that rush of slaughter the friend of the Scyldings rewarded me richly with ornamented gold and many treasures, once morning had come and we had sat down to the feast.
sentences.n: ‘lēanode’ is the past of ‘lēanian’, ‘reward’, which takes the dative of the person, ‘Mē’, while ‘þone wælrǣs’, ‘that onrush of slaughter’, is the accusative of what is rewarded (‘wælrǣse’ at 824). ‘wine Scildunga’ is ‘friend of the Scyldings’, Hrothgar. ‘fǣttan golde’ is a dative of means, ‘with adorned gold’: ‘fǣtt’ is ‘adorned, plated’, and ‘beaten’ or ‘ornamented’ gold is the sense I take from the lexica, a guess. ‘fela’ is the adverb ‘much’, and ‘manegum māðmum’ ‘with many treasures’ restates the means. ‘syððan mergen cōm’ is ‘after morning came’, and ‘wē tō symble geseten hæfdon’ is a pluperfect, ‘we had sat down to the feast’, with ‘symbel’ a ceremonial banquet. The morning meant is the one after Grendel’s last night.

sentences.t:
Þǣr wæs gidd ond glēo; gomela Scilding,
felafricgende feorran rehte;
sentences.l: There was tale and glee; the old Scylding, much-asking, from afar told;
sentences.i: There was storytelling and mirth; the old Scylding, who had learned much, told of things from far away;
sentences.n: ‘gidd ond glēo’ is ‘tale and glee’ (‘gidd’, ‘speech, tale’, as ‘gid’ at 1065; ‘glēo’ ‘mirth, music’). ‘gomela Scilding’ is ‘the old Scylding’, Hrothgar himself, as the next lines show, and he is the teller. ‘felafricgende’ is printed as one word, from ‘fela’, ‘much’, and ‘fricgende’, the present participle of ‘frignan’, ‘ask, learn by asking’, so ‘much-asking’ or ‘much-informed’; most editors print two words, ‘fela fricgende’ (apparatus), and the sense ‘one who has learned much’ is a guess. ‘feorran rehte’ is ‘from afar told’, ‘rehte’ the past of ‘reccan’ as in 2093; I take ‘feorran’ to mean tales of far places or far times, which is also a guess.

sentences.t:
hwīlum hildedēor hearpan wynne,
gomenwudu grētte, hwīlum gyd āwræc
sōð ond sārlīc, hwīlum syllīc spell
rehte æfter rihte rūmheort cyning;
sentences.l: at times the battle-brave one the harp’s joy, the joy-wood, greeted, at times a lay uttered, true and sorrowful, at times a wondrous tale told according to right the roomy-hearted king;
sentences.i: At times the battle-brave one struck the joy of the harp, that wood of delight; at times he uttered a lay, true and sorrowful; at times the large-hearted king told a marvellous tale, rightly as it should be told;
sentences.n: Three ‘hwīlum’ clauses, ‘at times … at times … at times’, run from 2107 to 2110 and a fourth follows at 2111, all with one subject: ‘hildedēor’, ‘battle-brave’, and ‘rūmheort cyning’, ‘roomy-hearted king’, both name Hrothgar, who plays and tells. ‘hearpan wynne’ is ‘the harp’s joy’, an accusative, and ‘gomenwudu’, ‘joy-wood’, is the same harp said again (as at 1065); ‘grētte’ is ‘greeted’, that is struck the strings. The italic ‘n’ of ‘gomenwudu’ marks a change: the manuscript reads ‘go/mel’ in the apparatus, apparently ‘gomel’, ‘old’, and Grundtvig’s ‘gomen-’ gives ‘joy-wood’. ‘gyd āwræc’ is ‘uttered a lay’ (‘āwrecan’, as ‘āwræc’ at 1724), ‘sōð ond sārlīc’ ‘true and sorrowful’. ‘syllīc spell’ is ‘wondrous tale’; Grein (with a query), Scheinert (with a query) and Holthausen would read ‘searolīc’, ‘cunning, skilful’, so the word is doubtful and my ‘wondrous’ is a choice. ‘æfter rihte’ is ‘according to right’, as it ought to be told.

sentences.l: at times again began, by age bound, the old war-man, of youth to lament, of battle-strength;
sentences.i: and again at times, held fast by age, the old man of war would begin to mourn his youth and his strength in battle;
sentences.n: ‘ongan’ is ‘began’ with the infinitive ‘cwīðan’ at the end of the clause, ‘lament’, and what he mourns is ‘gioguðe’, ‘youth’ (the ending ‘-e’ is that of the genitive or dative of ‘geoguð’, and ‘cwīðan’ is usually construed with the genitive), and ‘hildestrengo’, ‘battle-strength’ (‘hilde’ ‘battle’, ‘strengu’ ‘strength’); the ending ‘-o’ is the nominative or accusative form of ‘strengu’, not its regular genitive (‘strenge’), so I take it as a second object beside ‘gioguðe’, and the case of the pair is not settled. ‘gomel gūðwiga’ is ‘the old war-man’. ‘eldo gebunden’ is ‘bound by age’: I take ‘eldo’ as a form of ‘ieldu’, ‘age’, and ‘gebunden’ as ‘held fast’, as if shackled. The ending ‘-o’ is not the regular dative (which would be ‘ylde’), so reading it as ‘by age’ is a guess.

sentences.t:
hreðer inne wēoll,
þonne hē wintrum frōd worn gemunde.
sentences.l: the breast within welled, when he, wise with winters, a multitude remembered.
sentences.i: his heart surged within him whenever, wise with the years, he called so much to mind.
sentences.n: ‘hreðer inne wēoll’ is ‘the breast within welled’: ‘hreðer’ is ‘breast, heart’, and ‘wēoll’ the past of ‘weallan’, ‘well up, boil’, the verb used of the sea at 2138. ‘þonne’ is ‘when’ in the sense ‘whenever’, so the swelling comes each time. ‘wintrum frōd’ is ‘wise with winters’ (as at 1724), and ‘worn’ is ‘a multitude’, the object of ‘gemunde’, the past of ‘gemunan’, ‘remember’.

sentences.t:
Swā wē þǣr inne andlangne dæg
nīode nāman, oð ðæt niht becwōm
ōðer tō yldum.
sentences.l: So we there within the whole day long eagerly took, until night came, another, to men.
sentences.i: So we took our pleasure there within for the whole day long, until a second night came down on men.
sentences.n: ‘andlangne dæg’ is an accusative of time, ‘the whole day long’. ‘nīode nāman’ is ‘eagerly took’: ‘nīode’ is ‘eagerly, with zeal’ and ‘nāman’ is the plural past of ‘niman’, ‘take’, with no object stated; ‘took our pleasure’ is the sense I supply, a guess. ‘oð ðæt’ is ‘until’, ‘becwōm’ the past of ‘becuman’, ‘come’, and ‘ōðer’ ‘another’, a second night after the one in which Grendel came. ‘tō yldum’ is ‘to men’: ‘ylde’ is a plural noun for mankind.

sentences.l: Then was again quickly ready for grief-vengeance Grendel’s mother, journeyed sorrowful;
sentences.i: Then Grendel’s mother was soon ready once more to avenge her grief; she came, full of sorrow;
sentences.n: ‘gearo’, ‘ready’, takes the genitive ‘gyrnwræce’, ‘grief-vengeance’ (‘gyrn’ ‘grief, injury’, ‘wræc’ ‘vengeance’, as at 1138), so ‘ready for the avenging of her grief’. ‘Grendeles mōdor’ is the nominative subject. ‘eft hraðe’ is ‘again quickly’, ‘eft’ marking a second visitor to Heorot after Grendel. ‘sīðode’ is the past of ‘sīðian’, ‘go’, from ‘sīð’, ‘journey’, and ‘sorhfull’, ‘sorrow-full’, describes her.

sentences.t:
sunu dēað fornam,
wīghete Wedra.
sentences.l: son death took away, the war-hate of the Weders.
sentences.i: Death had taken her son, the Weders’ hatred in war.
sentences.n: ‘sunu dēað fornam’ is ‘death took the son’, ‘fornam’ the past of ‘forniman’, ‘take away’, with ‘sunu’ an accusative. ‘wīghete Wedra’ I take as a second nominative in apposition to ‘dēað’ (the form ‘wīghete’ is the same in the dative, which would give ‘through the Weders’ war-hate’): ‘wīg’ ‘war’, ‘hete’ ‘hate’, and ‘Wedra’ the genitive plural of ‘Wederas’, the Weders, the Geats, so the hatred meant is Beowulf’s people’s.

sentences.l: A monstrous woman her child avenged, a warrior killed boldly;
sentences.i: That monstrous woman avenged her child, and killed a warrior with courage;
sentences.n: ‘Wīf unhȳre’ is ‘a monstrous woman’: ‘unhȳre’ is ‘un-’ with ‘hȳre’, ‘gentle, pleasant’, so ‘ungentle, uncanny, horrible’. One subject has two verbs: ‘gewræc’, past of ‘gewrecan’, ‘avenge’, with ‘hyre bearn’, ‘her child’, as object, and ‘ācwealde’, past of ‘ācwellan’, ‘kill’, with ‘beorn’, ‘warrior’. ‘ellenlīce’ is the adverb ‘boldly’. The warrior is named in the next unit.

sentences.t:
þǣr wæs Æschere,
frōdan fyrnwitan feorh ūðgenge.
sentences.l: there was to Æschere, to the wise ancient-counsellor, life departing.
sentences.i: There the life was going out of Æschere, the wise old counsellor.
sentences.n: ‘Æschere’ and ‘frōdan fyrnwitan’ are datives, ‘to Æschere, to the wise ancient-counsellor’: ‘frōd’ is ‘wise’ and ‘fyrnwita’ is ‘fyrn’, ‘ancient’, with ‘wita’, ‘counsellor’. ‘feorh ūðgenge’ is ‘life departing’; ‘ūðgenge’ is a rare adjective, ‘going away’, and the construction ‘there was to X life departing’ is my reading, a guess. Æschere is Hrothgar’s chief counsellor, Yrmenlaf’s elder brother, whose death Hrothgar mourns at 1323.

sentences.t:
Nōðer hȳ hine ne mōston, syððan mergen cwōm,
dēaðwērigne Denia lēode
bronde forbærnan, nē on bę̄l hladan,
lēofne mannan;
sentences.l: Neither they him were allowed, after morning came, the death-weary one, the Danes’ people, with brand to burn up, nor on pyre to lay, the dear man;
sentences.i: The people of the Danes were not allowed, once morning had come, to burn him with fire, weary with death as he was, or to lay the dear man on the pyre;
sentences.n: ‘Nōðer hȳ hine ne mōston … nē’ is ‘neither could they … nor’, the negatives piled up; ‘mōston’ is the past plural of ‘mōtan’, ‘be allowed’, and ‘hȳ’ ‘they’ is restated by ‘Denia lēode’, ‘the people of the Danes’ (‘Denia’ the genitive plural of ‘Dene’). ‘dēaðwērigne’ is ‘death-weary’, an accusative with ‘hine’, ‘him’, and ‘lēofne mannan’, ‘the dear man’, is Æschere again. ‘bronde’ is the dative of ‘brond’, ‘brand’, ‘with the burning brand’, and ‘forbærnan’ ‘burn up’; ‘hladan’ is ‘to lay’, literally ‘load’. In ‘bę̄l’ the ‘ę̄’ is e caudata, which the manuscript writes; most editors print ‘bǣl’, ‘pyre’, and Holthausen and Chambers keep the form (apparatus). The Danes burned their dead, and here the body was taken out of their reach.

sentences.t:
hīo þæt līc ætbær
fēondes fæð(mum un)der firgenstrēam.
sentences.l: she that body bore away, in the fiend’s embrace, under the mountain-stream.
sentences.i: She had carried the body off in the fiend’s clasp, beneath the mountain stream.
sentences.n: ‘hīo’ is ‘she’ (the Thorkelin transcripts have ‘hio’) and ‘ætbær’ the past of ‘ætberan’, ‘carry off’, with ‘þæt līc’, ‘that body’, as object. ‘fēondes fæð(mum un)der’ is ‘in the fiend’s embrace under’: ‘fēondes’ is a genitive, ‘fæðm’ is ‘embrace, grasp’, and ‘fæðmum’ a dative plural. The manuscript has only ‘fæð’ and then a gap; the parenthesised letters ‘mum un’ are restored from Grein’s second edition, and Kemble proposed ‘fæðrunga’ with ‘under’. ‘firgenstrēam’ is ‘mountain-stream’ (‘fyrgenstrēam’ at 1359), the water of the mere, so she carried him down beneath it.

sentences.t:
Þæt wæs Hrōðgāre hrēowa tornost
þāra þe lēodfruman lange begēate.
sentences.l: That was to Hrothgar of griefs the bitterest, of those which long had befallen the people-chief.
sentences.i: That was the bitterest to Hrothgar of all the griefs that had long come upon the leader of his people.
sentences.n: ‘hrēowa tornost’ is ‘the bitterest of griefs’: ‘tornost’ is the superlative of ‘torn’, ‘bitter, grievous’, and ‘hrēowa’ the genitive plural of ‘hrēow’, ‘grief’, a genitive of the group. ‘Hrōðgāre’ is a dative, ‘to Hrothgar’. In the relative clause ‘þāra þe lēodfruman lange begēate’, ‘þāra’ is ‘of those’ and ‘þe’ ‘which’; ‘begēate’ is the past subjunctive of ‘begietan’, ‘get, befall’, and ‘lēodfruman’, ‘people-chief’ (‘lēod’ ‘people’, ‘fruma’ ‘beginner, chief’), I take as its accusative object, ‘had long befallen the chief’. That parsing is a guess, because ‘lēodfruman’ ends in ‘-an’, which is accusative, dative or genitive alike.

sentences.t:
Þā se ðēoden mec ðīne līfe
healsode hrēohmōd, þæt ic on holma geþring
eorlscipe efnde, ealdre genēðde,
mǣrðo fremede;
sentences.l: Then the lord me, by your life, begged, fierce-minded, that I in the throng of the waves noble-deed performed, with life ventured, glories accomplished;
sentences.i: Then the king, troubled in mind, besought me by your life that I should do a hero’s work in the press of the waves, venture my life, and achieve glory;
sentences.n: ‘ðīne līfe’ is a crux. ‘ðīne’ is ‘your’ and ‘līfe’ the dative of ‘līf’, ‘life’, but the endings disagree (a dative would be ‘ðīnum’), and the phrase may be an oath, ‘by your life’, with ‘your’ meaning Higelāc, or ‘for your life’, ‘on your account’; I render ‘by your life’, a guess. ‘healsode’ is the past of ‘healsian’, ‘beseech’ (perhaps from ‘heals’, ‘neck’, as if clasping the neck), and ‘hrēohmōd’ is ‘fierce-minded’ in ‘l’: ‘hrēoh’ is ‘stormy, rough, fierce’, and ‘i’ puts it as ‘troubled in mind’, the storm being Hrothgar’s grief. ‘þæt ic … efnde, … genēðde, … fremede’ is the request in the past subjunctive: ‘efnde’ from ‘efnan’, ‘perform’, ‘genēðde’ from ‘genēðan’, ‘risk’, ‘fremede’ from ‘fremman’, ‘accomplish’. ‘on holma geþring’ is ‘in the throng of the waves’ (‘holm’ ‘sea’), ‘eorlscipe’ ‘a hero’s deeds’, ‘ealdre’ a dative, ‘with my life’, and ‘mǣrðo’ ‘glories’.

sentences.t: hē mē mēde gehēt.
sentences.l: he me reward promised.
sentences.i: He promised me a reward.
sentences.n: ‘gehēt’ is the past of ‘gehātan’, ‘promise’, with the dative ‘mē’, ‘to me’, and ‘mēde’, ‘reward’ (‘mēd’), the thing promised. The promise is kept at 2101–2104, and again at 2142.

sentences.t:
Ic ðā ðæs wælmes, þē is wīde cūð,
grimne gryrelīcne grundhyrde fond.
sentences.l: I then of that surge, which is widely known, the grim, dreadful ground-guardian found.
sentences.i: Then I found the grim and dreadful guardian of the depths of that surge, which is known far and wide.
sentences.n: ‘Ic ðā … fond’ is ‘I then found’, ‘fond’ the past of ‘findan’. The object is ‘grundhyrde’, ‘ground-guardian’ (‘grund’ ‘bottom’, ‘hyrde’ ‘keeper’, as in ‘fyrena hyrde’), the creature of the mere’s floor, here the mother (compare ‘grundwyrgenne’ at 1518). ‘ðæs wælmes’ is a genitive, ‘of that surge’, ‘wælm’ being ‘welling, surge’, and ‘þē is wīde cūð’ is ‘which is widely known’, ‘þē’ the relative. ‘grimne gryrelīcne’ are masculine accusatives, ‘grim, dreadful’, with no ‘and’; the masculine ending is used of the mother as ‘sē’ was at 1497. The italic ‘ne’ of ‘grimne’ marks a change: the manuscript reads ‘grimme’, and Thorpe’s ‘grimne’ is the accusative that agrees with ‘grundhyrde’.

sentences.t: Þǣr unc hwīle wæs hand gemǣne;
sentences.l: There to us two for a while was hand in common;
sentences.i: There for a while it was hand to hand between the two of us;
sentences.n: ‘unc’ is the dative dual, ‘to us two’ (Beowulf and the monster; compare ‘uncer’ at 2002), and ‘hwīle’ an accusative of time, ‘for a while’. ‘hand gemǣne’ is ‘hand common’: ‘gemǣne’ is ‘shared, in common’, and I take the phrase to mean fighting hand to hand, blows given and taken. Grundtvig, Kemble, Chambers and others print it as a single word ‘hand-gemǣne’ (apparatus), so whether it is a compound or an adjective with its noun is open, and the sense is a guess.

sentences.l: the sea with gore welled, and I at the head cut down in that [war]-hall Grendel’s mother with mighty edges;
sentences.i: the water seethed with blood, and in that hall of war I cut Grendel’s mother down at the head with the mighty blade;
sentences.n: ‘holm heolfre wēoll’ is ‘the sea welled with gore’: ‘holm’ is the nominative, ‘heolfre’ a dative of means, and ‘wēoll’ the verb of 2113. ‘ic hēafde becearf Grendeles mōdor’ is ‘I cut Grendel’s mother at the head’: ‘becearf’ is the past of ‘becorfan’, ‘cut off, cut down’, ‘Grendeles mōdor’ the object, and ‘hēafde’ a dative, ‘at the head’ (whether she was struck on the head or beheaded is not settled by the word); at 1567 the blow breaks her ‘bānhringas’, the neck-bones, so this is Beowulf’s looser retelling. The same construction at 1590, ‘hine hēafde becearf’, is rendered in the earlier part ‘cut him off from his head’, so ‘hēafde’ here may be a dative of what is cut off and the sense ‘beheaded’; I keep ‘at the head’ because the poem has her struck, not beheaded. ‘ēacnum ecgum’ is ‘with mighty edges’, ‘ēacen’ being ‘enlarged, mighty’, a plural for the one blade. The brackets of ‘[gūð]sele’ mark ‘gūð’ as Klaeber’s addition: ‘gūðsele’ is ‘war-hall’, the word used of Heorot at 443, and Thorpe, Holthausen, Sedgefield and others read ‘gūð-’, while Grundtvig, Schücking and Chambers read ‘[grund-]’, ‘ground-hall’, so the reading is doubtful; ‘nīðsele’ at 1513 is the comparison Klaeber cites for the form.

sentences.t:
unsōfte þonan
feorh oðferede;
sentences.l: with difficulty thence life carried off;
sentences.i: I carried my life away from there only with difficulty;
sentences.n: ‘unsōfte’ is the adverb ‘un-softly’, ‘with difficulty’, ‘þonan’ ‘from there’, and ‘feorh’, ‘life’, is the object of ‘oðferede’, the past of ‘oðferian’, ‘carry away’ (‘oð-’ ‘away’, ‘ferian’ ‘carry’). The subject ‘ic’ is carried over from the previous clause.

sentences.t: næs ic fǣge þā gȳt;
sentences.l: was-not I doomed then yet;
sentences.i: I was not yet fated to die;
sentences.n: ‘næs’ is ‘ne wæs’, ‘was not’, with ‘ic’ after it, and ‘fǣge’ is ‘doomed to die’, as in the earlier parts; ‘fated’ is the sense that suits the poem. ‘þā gȳt’ is ‘then yet’, ‘even then’, so ‘not yet’. ‘doomed’ is the choice I make among these senses, as in the earlier parts.

sentences.t:
ac mē eorla hlēo eft gesealde
māðma menigeo, maga Healfdenes.
sentences.l: but to me the shelter of earls again gave a multitude of treasures, the kinsman of Healfdene.
sentences.i: but the protector of earls, Healfdene’s son, gave me many treasures again.
sentences.n: ‘ac’ is ‘but’, and ‘mē’ is the dative, ‘to me’, of ‘gesealde’, ‘gave’; ‘eft’ is ‘again’, the second gift after the one at 2102. ‘eorla hlēo’ is ‘shelter of earls’ and ‘maga Healfdenes’ ‘kinsman of Healfdene’, that is his son (‘maga’ ‘son, kinsman’), both Hrothgar. ‘māðma menigeo’ is ‘a multitude of treasures’: ‘menigeo’ is a feminine noun, ‘multitude’, and ‘māðma’ the genitive plural. The sentence ends at the full stop of 2143.
